params.question: A patient with a mediastinal mass presents with facial swelling, distended non-pulsatile neck veins, and visible collateral veins across the chest wall. Which mechanism best explains this clinical picture?

answers.text: Compression of the trachea causing airway obstruction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Tracheal compression causes cough, breathlessness, or stridor — not facial swelling or venous distension. These are airway symptoms, not venous signs.

answers.text: Obstruction of the superior vena cava impeding venous return

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The superior vena cava returns all blood from the upper body to the heart. A mediastinal mass compressing it raises venous pressure in the head, neck, and arms, producing facial plethora, non-pulsatile neck vein distension, and chest wall collaterals.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement causes hoarseness due to vocal cord paralysis. It does not produce facial swelling or venous changes.
Inappropriate ADH secretion causes hyponatraemia and fluid retention, but not the localised mechanical pattern of facial oedema with non-pulsatile venous distension seen here.

overallFeedback.feedback: This presentation is SVC obstruction — the mass compresses the superior vena cava, blocking venous return from the upper body. The hallmarks are facial oedema, non-pulsatile neck vein distension, and visible chest wall collaterals.
Correct! SVC obstruction is a key compressive complication of mediastinal masses. The non-pulsatile nature of the neck vein distension distinguishes it from cardiac causes.

interactions.label: A patient with a Pancoast tumour at the lung apex presents with ipsilateral ptos

params.question: A patient with a Pancoast tumour at the lung apex presents with ipsilateral ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis. Which anatomical structure has the tumour invaded to produce these signs?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Brachial plexus invasion by a Pancoast tumour causes shoulder and arm pain, not the Horner syndrome triad. Both structures are affected at the apex, but they produce different clinical features.
The phrenic nerve innervates the diaphragm. Its involvement causes diaphragm paralysis and breathlessness, not ptosis, miosis, or anhidrosis.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement causes hoarseness through vocal cord paralysis. It runs through the mediastinum, not at the lung apex.

The sympathetic chain runs alongside the vertebral column at the lung apex. A Pancoast tumour invading this chain disrupts sympathetic innervation to the ipsilateral face, producing the classic Horner syndrome: ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis.

overallFeedback.feedback: The triad of ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis is Horner syndrome, caused by invasion of the sympathetic chain at the lung apex. The brachial plexus, also at the apex, produces the shoulder and arm pain component of Pancoast syndrome.

Correct! Horner syndrome results from sympathetic chain invasion. Remember that a Pancoast tumour also typically invades the brachial plexus, causing shoulder and arm pain — both are hallmarks of an apical lung tumour.

params.question: A 45-year-old man has an anterior mediastinal mass on chest X-ray. Contrast-enhanced CT confirms a solid lesion, and serum alpha-fetoprotein is elevated. What is the most important next step before deciding on treatment?

answers.text: Proceed directly to surgical excision based on imaging

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Operating without tissue diagnosis is inappropriate. An anterior mediastinal mass that looks resectable may turn out to be lymphoma, which requires chemotherapy — not surgery. Histology must come first.

answers.text: Order a PET-CT scan to stage the disease

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Staging (step 5) follows tissue diagnosis (step 4) in the investigation ladder. Without knowing the cell type, staging cannot guide treatment selection.

answers.text: Obtain a tissue biopsy for histological diagnosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Tissue diagnosis is the non-negotiable step. Elevated AFP suggests a germ-cell tumour, but tumour markers alone do not replace histological confirmation. The cell type determines whether the patient needs surgery, chemotherapy, or radiotherapy.

answers.text: Start empirical chemotherapy given the raised tumour marker

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Treating without tissue confirmation risks managing the wrong disease. Even with a suggestive tumour marker, histological diagnosis must precede treatment — the cell type determines the entire management pathway.

overallFeedback.feedback: The investigation ladder requires tissue diagnosis before treatment. Regardless of how suggestive the imaging or tumour markers are, the cell type must be confirmed histologically because it determines the entire management pathway.

Correct! Tissue diagnosis is step four of the investigation ladder and is non-negotiable. The cell type — not the imaging or tumour markers — determines whether the patient goes to theatre or to oncology.

interactions.label: An anterior mediastinal mass appears completely resectable on CT imaging. Which

params.question: An anterior mediastinal mass appears completely resectable on CT imaging. Which tissue diagnosis would most appropriately shift primary management from surgical excision to chemotherapy with radiotherapy?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Thymoma is treated by thymectomy (surgical removal of the thymus). It is a surgical disease, and resection can also improve associated myasthenia gravis.
Mature teratomas are benign germ-cell tumours treated by surgical excision. Their management remains surgical when the mass is resectable.

Lymphoma is the critical exception. Even when an anterior mediastinal mass appears resectable, biopsy-confirmed lymphoma requires chemotherapy combined with radiotherapy as primary treatment — not surgery. This is why tissue diagnosis must always precede any operative decision.
Schwannomas are posterior mediastinal neurogenic tumours arising from nerve sheaths. They are treated by surgical resection and would not typically present in the anterior compartment.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key exception to remember: lymphoma requires chemotherapy and radiotherapy as primary treatment, even when the mass appears resectable on imaging. Thymoma, teratoma, and neurogenic tumours are managed surgically — but lymphoma is not.

Correct! Lymphoma can mimic a surgically resectable mass, but taking it straight to theatre is inappropriate. Chemotherapy and radiotherapy are the primary treatment — this underscores why tissue biopsy is mandatory before any management decision.
